name: Potassium azeloyl diglycinate

lead: Potassium azeloyl diglycinate (PAD) is a derivative of azelaic acid that dissolves in water and is used in cosmetic creams and serums. It is aimed at reducing facial redness and uneven pigmentation, which makes skin look calmer and more even.
Small studies have tested PAD-containing creams in rosacea and melasma and report reduced erythema and pigment.

paras: PAD is a leave-on ingredient, usually applied twice daily in trials, and is often combined with other actives such as hydroxypropyl chitosan or niacinamide. Trial periods ran from four to twelve weeks.
Studies of PAD-containing creams report them as well tolerated, with trials focused on reduced stinging and burning. Results come from small studies of combination products.

angle.text: People use PAD-containing creams to reduce facial redness and fade dark patches. It is an ingredient in formulated products rather than a standalone treatment.

lead: Potassium azeloyl diglycinate is a salt of azelaic acid linked to glycine, marketed as Azeloglicina and used in cosmetic formulations [1]. Its appeal is that it is water-soluble, unlike azelaic acid, which makes it easier to use in light creams and gels.

In appearance terms, it is used for redness and for hyperpigmentation. A randomized trial of 42 rosacea patients applying a cream with 5% PAD and 1% hydroxypropyl chitosan twice daily for four weeks reported reduced erythema measured by Mexameter [1]. An open multicenter study of 37 patients treated 12 weeks reported soothing of stinging and burning [2].

In melasma, a Thai randomized controlled trial tested a combination of tranexamic-acid derivative, PAD and niacinamide for eight weeks, assessing melanin differences [3]. Because all trials use combination products, effects cannot be assigned to PAD alone.

paras: In a randomized multicenter double-blind study, 42 patients with stage I-II rosacea used a cream with 5% PAD and 1% HPCH twice daily; erythema decreased instrumentally and clinically over 28 days [1]. An open study of 37 patients over 12 weeks found a soothing effect [2].
A single-center randomized study in Thai adults compared a combination emulsion containing PAD with a control over 8 weeks with SPF 30 sunscreen for all [3].
Laboratory studies examine PAD in hydrogels with tetracyclines and in anti-acne preparations [4][5].
Trials are listed above; they are small and test combination products [1][3][2].
